transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I’m Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well… I suppose I came in because I’ve had this feeling that’s hard to shake. Not dramatic, exactly, but it’s there—like the best part of my life may already be behind me. I used to think if I stayed organized, made a plan, kept some discipline, I could get myself back on track.

I was always pretty good at that, actually—planning things out, keeping routines. In graduate school I practically lived by lists, color-coded folders, all of that. But lately it feels like none of that really gets me back to feeling like myself. It’s a quiet sort of hopelessness, I guess. Stubborn. That’s what finally made me think I should talk to someone.
Have you noticed that you don’t take pleasure in things anymore—activities or hobbies you used to enjoy?

I’m not sure, honestly. I still do some things I’ve always done, though whether I’d call it “pleasure” is… hard to say. I used to have a pretty clear sense of what I enjoyed, but now I sometimes wonder if I’m just doing things because they’re part of the routine.

I suppose that happens as you get older too—your days narrow a bit. When I retired, I thought I’d have all this time to revisit interests, but time is funny that way. It fills up with errands and appointments and reading the news too long. So… I don’t know that I’ve noticed a specific hobby becoming joyless, exactly. I just don’t feel as certain about what I enjoy anymore.
Would you say that you feel down or sad most days, even if it’s not intensely dramatic?

Yes… most days, I think so. Not in a dramatic way—I’m not crying at breakfast or unable to speak to anyone—but there’s this low, gray sort of tone underneath things.

Even if I’m in the studio, or sitting across from my wife at dinner, it’s still there. Funny, I used to pay attention to light and color more—well, I still do, I suppose—but now everything feels a little muted. So yes, down most days, just quietly.
Have you noticed that you feel tired or lacking in energy most days, even if you haven’t been doing much physically?

Yes, I think so. I mean, I still get up and do what needs doing—the shopping, little errands, tinkering with projects around the house or in the studio. I’m not just lying around all day.

But it’s odd… things that shouldn’t take much out of me do. Setting things up for a mentoring session, for example—just getting materials together, making sure the chairs are right, that sort of thing—can leave me feeling worn out. Or if I walk through one of those community events, even briefly, afterward I feel drained in a way that lying down for a bit doesn’t really fix. A nap helps in the usual way, I suppose, but it doesn’t make me feel restored.
Have you noticed any changes in your ability to think clearly, concentrate, or make decisions lately?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed anything definite there. I mean, I have the usual moments of walking into a room and forgetting why I went in—though my wife says everyone our age does that, and she’s probably right.

Decisions… I don’t know. I’ve never been especially quick with decisions. Even choosing a frame for an old print can become an entire afternoon if I let it. But that’s always been me, I think. Concentration comes and goes depending on what I’m doing. If something catches me, I can stay with it for a while; if it doesn’t, my mind wanders to other things. So… I wouldn’t say there’s been a clear change lately, no.
How long have you been feeling this way—this low, gray tone underneath things?

It really began after the hiking injury… a little over three years ago now. Funny, I can still picture the trail—more clearly than I can picture what I had for lunch yesterday—but yes, that’s when the grayness seemed to settle in.

So… about three years and three months, give or take. It’s been long enough that I’ve almost gotten used to it, which is a strange thing to say.
Looking back, would you say that there have been times when you no longer found pleasure in things you used to truly enjoy, even for a moment?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way exactly. I mean, I still do things I’ve always liked—or I try to. Sometimes the enjoyment is quieter than it used to be, but whether that’s “no pleasure” or just… getting older, or being tired of the same routines, I don’t know.

I used to spend ages fussing over old tools, little repairs, that sort of thing. And I still can get absorbed in it sometimes. Though then I’ll notice a drawer needs sorting, and that reminds me of my father’s workbench—he had this way of keeping every screw in a coffee tin, completely impossible to find anything, but he knew where it all was. Funny how that comes back.

So, I don’t know. I wouldn’t say I have a clean answer. There may be moments where things feel a bit flat, but I’m not sure I’d say I stopped finding pleasure in them.
Looking back, have you ever felt that even the things you used to truly enjoy felt flat or uninteresting, even for a short while?

I’m not sure, honestly. “Flat or uninteresting” is a strong way to put it. I can think of afternoons where I’ve sat down with something I usually like and just sort of… didn’t get much from it. But then sometimes I’ll come back to it later and it’s fine enough.

It’s hard to separate from the ordinary ebb and flow, you know? My wife can watch the same old film and enjoy it every time, and I start noticing the wallpaper in the scene or wondering what year the car is. That doesn’t necessarily mean I’m not enjoying it—I just drift.

So I don’t know that I can give you a clear yes. Maybe things feel muted sometimes, but I wouldn’t say I’ve completely lost interest in them.
Looking back, have you had times when even the things you used to care about felt like they didn’t matter as much, even if just for a while?

I’m not sure I’ve thought of it in terms of “mattering.” That word feels a little bigger than what I’d say. There are days when I don’t get around to things I used to care about, or I look at them and think, well, that can wait. But I don’t know if that means they matter less, exactly.

I still care about the same sorts of things, I think. It’s just sometimes they don’t pull me toward them the way they used to. Though then again, I’ll suddenly spend an hour looking for some old chisel because I remember the handle had a crack in it, and then I’m annoyed if I can’t find it. So clearly some part of me still cares.

Sorry, I’m going around the houses. I don’t have a clear yes or no. More like… sometimes things feel a bit dulled, but I wouldn’t say they stop mattering.
